title: Generative Design and Graph Neural Network Screening of Novel Bimetallic Alloy Catalysts for the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
authors: Vipin Kurian Elavunkel, Sylvain Le Tonquesse, Hadrien Vroylandt
abstract: Identifying earth-abundant catalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is a central challenge in scalable green hydrogen production. We present a computational pipeline that couples diffusion-based generative modelling, machine-learning force-field relaxation, and graph neural network (GNN) property prediction to discover bimetallic HER catalysts beyond the structures and stoichiometries covered by existing adsorption databases. A generative model (MatterGen) is fine-tuned on bulk alloy structures labelled with their minimum hydrogen adsorption energy and steered towards adsorption energies near zero. From the generated pool we retain the stable structures that are novel bimetallic alloys: binary compositions built from the training-set metals but at stoichiometries or structures absent from that database. Each candidate's low-index facets are ranked by a machine-learning-force-field (MatterSim) surface-energy screen, and only the most stable terminations are converted into explicit slab models with hydrogen adsorbed at all high-symmetry surface sites and relaxed with the same force field. Two GNN surrogates (MEGNet and ALIGNN), trained on a high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) dataset, then screen the resulting slab candidates. Because the two models encode the local environment through different inductive biases, we retain only the alloys on which both agree, reducing the influence of any single model. This consensus screening, combined with a MatterSim energy-difference triangulation, resulted in a shortlist of near-thermoneutral bimetallic candidates. Eight are validated with plane-wave DFT, and four of them, Pd5Au, Pt5Rh, Cu5Pt3, and Pd13Ru3, bind hydrogen within the thermoneutral window. All eight alloys are dynamically stable by phonon calculations. These four alloys are highlighted as DFT-validated bimetallic HER candidates for experimental follow-up.

infographic.key_insight: Generative design and consensus GNN screening identified four novel bimetallic HER candidates with DFT-validated near-thermoneutral hydrogen binding: Pd5Au, Pt5Rh, Cu5Pt3, and Pd13Ru3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The pipeline narrows computational searches to promising alloy compositions and surfaces for experimental hydrogen-evolution catalyst development.
method: Fine-tune MatterGen on adsorption-labelled bulk alloys to generate novel binaries targeting near-zero hydrogen adsorption energy.
Use MatterSim to screen surface stability and relax hydrogen-adsorbed slabs at high-symmetry sites.
Combine MEGNet–ALIGNN consensus with MatterSim energy checks, then validate shortlisted alloys using DFT and phonons.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of eight shortlisted alloys evaluated with plane-wave DFT, four met the thermoneutral hydrogen-binding criterion, and all eight were dynamically stable in phonon calculations.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental HER activity and durability remain unverified, and the four highlighted candidates contain precious metals despite the earth-abundance motivation.
infographic.paper_title: Generative Design and Graph Neural Network Screening of Novel Bimetallic Alloy Catalysts for the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction

title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science
authors: Xuwei Liu, Zhimin Zhang, Xiaoguang Hu, Zhongwei Liu, Yuanhui Sun, Jun Huo
abstract: Machine learning supports materials design, atomistic simulation and experimental characterization, yet models and workflows remain fragmented. We present PaddleMaterials, an open-source framework integrating heterogeneous materials-learning tasks while preserving task-specific representations and scientific semantics. It unifies data processing, training, evaluation, pretrained-model management and workflows across six task classes: property prediction, structure generation, machine-learning interatomic potentials, electronic-structure fields, spectrum elucidation and microscopy image processing. Task interfaces record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references, making cross-task composition verifiable. A shared compiler backend enables switching from dynamic-graph to compiled execution through one setting, using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation without changing model definitions. Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compiled execution accelerated every instance in eight groups, with group median speedups of 11%-224% and group maximum speedups of 11%-336%. Case studies on LiMnO2 and toluene link structure generation or spectrum elucidation, interatomic-potential relaxation, property prediction and electron-density prediction, using same-geometry density functional theory (DFT) calculations as references. For LiMnO2, predicted formation energies for generated and relaxed structures differed from same-geometry PBE+U references by at most 7 meV per atom, while the computational cost of model steps was less than one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation. PaddleMaterials extends unified materials workflows beyond conventional property, potential and structure-generation tasks while supporting verifiable cross-task operations and compiled execution.

infographic.key_insight: PaddleMaterials unifies six materials-learning task classes into verifiable workflows while supporting compiled execution without changing model definitions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can connect materials generation, relaxation and property analysis through shared infrastructure with explicit physical quantities, units and reference conventions.
method: Unify data processing, training, evaluation and pretrained-model management across six task classes.
Record scientific semantics in task interfaces to verify cross-task composition.
Enable compiled execution through one setting using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compilation accelerated every instance in eight groups; LiMnO2 formation-energy predictions differed from same-geometry PBE+U references by at most 7 meV/atom, with model-step costs below one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation.
infographic.watch_item: Compilation gains were not universal across all groups, and the reported case studies do not establish accuracy across broader material chemistries.
infographic.paper_title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science

title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction
authors: YuJie Liu, Dezhen Xue, Jun Sun, Xiangdong Ding, Zhibin Gao, Turab Lookman
abstract: As general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini and DeepSeek, exhibit increasingly advanced reasoning capabilities, a critical question arises: how do their property prediction abilities compare to those of domain-specific pretrained materials models? In this study, we evaluate predictions for Ti, steels, high-entropy alloy (HEA) and Al, demonstrating that general-purpose LLMs surprisingly outperform SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT. To further enhance performance, we introduce a hybrid approach that utilizes numerical priors from a prior model, such as CatBoost or SteelBERT, to guide the general LLMs (Deepseek V3.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash). By inputting these initial estimates from a prior model as prompts, the LLM acts as a reasoning corrector, achieving accuracy superior to the prior model and "unguided mode". Furthermore, we investigate the impact of data strategy using a similarity-based metric, revealing that data quality dominates quantity; using merely 5% of high-similarity reference data of training set as input yields performance similar to the results of using 100% of training set. Additionally, the LLMs demonstrate excellent uncertainty calibration, where self-reported "high" confidence strongly correlates with minimal deviation from ground truth. Our findings suggest that synergizing general-purpose LLMs with prior model numerical baselines and high-quality data curation creates a cost-effective and accurate paradigm for materials discovery, reducing the need for expensive domain-specific pretraining.

infographic.key_insight: General-purpose LLMs outperform domain-specific pretrained models in the reported alloy-property benchmarks, with further gains from numerical predictions supplied as prompts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining existing property predictors with general-purpose LLMs could improve alloy screening accuracy while reducing reliance on costly domain-specific pretraining.
method: Benchmark general-purpose LLMs against SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT on Ti, steel, high-entropy alloy, and Al datasets.
Prompt DeepSeek V3.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash with CatBoost or SteelBERT predictions to guide corrections.
Evaluate similarity-based reference-data selection and self-reported prediction confidence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that using only 5% of high-similarity training references achieves performance similar to using the full training set, while high self-reported confidence correlates with smaller prediction errors.
infographic.watch_item: Validate performance and confidence calibration on independently held-out, distribution-shifted alloys before relying on predictions for engineering decisions.
infographic.paper_title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction

title: Site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer for symmetry-constrained crystal generation
authors: Junchi Liu, Haoran Si, Luo Yan, Sergei Tretiak, Liujiang Zhou
abstract: Generative models for crystal structure prediction (CSP) have expanded the search space for novel materials and improved screening efficiency. However, simultaneously generating stable and novel structures remains challenging because of the complex structural and physical constraints governing crystals. To address this challenge, we propose site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer model (ST2M), a symmetry-guided discrete--continuous diffusion framework incorporating degree-of-freedom masks and conditioned on Wyckoff patterns. ST2M represents crystal structures as sequences of independent occupied Wyckoff orbits and employs a twin-branch Transformer to jointly denoise discrete and continuous variables. In our experiments, ST2M achieves a structural validity of 96.37\%. For known patterns in dataset, 23.86\% of generated structures simultaneously satisfy stability, uniqueness, and novelty criteria, representing a relative improvement of 68.15\% over the best-performing baseline. First-principles calculations identify a total of 21 previously unreported stable structures among selected candidates with low predicted energies. These results demonstrate that ST2M can generate chemically viable crystal candidates under prescribed crystallographic constraints and generalize to unknown Wyckoff patterns, providing a practical route to accelerated materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: ST2M guides crystal generation with crystallographic symmetry, improving the yield of structures that are simultaneously stable, unique, and novel.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Generating candidates under prescribed crystallographic constraints could accelerate materials screening and reduce wasted downstream calculations.
method: Represent crystals as sequences of independent occupied Wyckoff orbits.
Condition discrete–continuous diffusion on Wyckoff patterns and apply degree-of-freedom masks.
Use a twin-branch Transformer to jointly denoise discrete and continuous variables.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 96.37% structural validity, a 23.86% stable–unique–novel yield for known patterns (68.15% relative improvement over the best baseline), and 21 previously unreported stable structures identified by first-principles calculations among selected candidates.
infographic.watch_item: First-principles validation covered selected low-predicted-energy candidates; the abstract does not quantify performance on unknown Wyckoff patterns.
infographic.paper_title: Site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer for symmetry-constrained crystal generation

title: Atomistic Insights into MOCVD Growth of GaAs using a Closed Loop Autonomous System Combining Directed Reinforcement Learning and Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations
authors: Hrishi V. Harsora, Ashutosh Krishna Amaram, Raghavan Ranganathan, Tarun K. Agarwal
abstract: Conventional process optimization of the Metal-Organic Chemical Vapor Deposition (MOCVD) growth parameters to achieve high-quality thin films relies on iterative, resource-intensive experimental runs. While predictive modeling can circumvent this cost and effort, simulating thin-film growth is constrained by the vastly different length and time scales of the deposition process. While continuum (e.g., Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)) and first-principles methods (e.g., Molecular Dynamics (MD)) struggle to balance experimental length/time scales and atomistic accuracy, Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) bridges this divide by resolving atomistic events whilst remaining tractable at experimental length and time scales. However, the accuracy of KMC relies on kinetic rate parameters that require costly density functional theory (DFT) calculations. In order to circumvent this, we present a framework that calibrates the rate parameters directly against experimental growth data. A forward KMC growth model is coupled in a closed loop with a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) optimizer that navigates the high-dimensional parameter space, with the search steered by the degree of rate control of each reaction rate parameter. The approach invokes no material-specific assumptions and hence, any deposition process whose forward kinetics can be reduced to a set of rate-controlled events is amenable to the same treatment. We demonstrate it for the MOCVD of GaAs, where the calibrated model captures the characteristic temperature dependence of the measured growth rate. The framework is also able to recover the three well known kinetic regimes characterized by change in the rate determining step from precursor chemisorption to desorption. As a result, the framework converts routinely measured growth data into a mechanistically interpretable model of the deposition process.

infographic.key_insight: A closed-loop optimizer calibrates atomistic GaAs growth kinetics directly from experimental growth data, reducing reliance on costly DFT-derived rate parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support MOCVD process optimization by turning routine growth measurements into a mechanistically interpretable deposition model.
method: Simulate atomistic deposition events with kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC).
Use Monte Carlo Tree Search to calibrate kinetic rate parameters against experimental growth data.
Guide parameter searches using each reaction’s degree of rate control.
infographic.evidence_signal: For GaAs MOCVD, the calibrated model captures the measured growth-rate dependence on temperature and recovers three known kinetic regimes with changing rate-determining steps.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer to other deposition processes requires a suitable rate-controlled event model; the abstract reports validation only for GaAs.
infographic.paper_title: Atomistic Insights into MOCVD Growth of GaAs using a Closed Loop Autonomous System Combining Directed Reinforcement Learning and Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations

title: Triboelectric nanogenerators across length scales: linking materials, multiscale modelling and applications
authors: MD Tanzib Ehsan Sanglap, Ans Al Rashid, Abdullah Sayam, Injamamul Arief, Andrei G. Shvarts, Lukasz Kaczmarczyk
abstract: Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert low-frequency mechanical energy into electricity and enable self-powered sensing. Their performance depends on interactions among material properties, surface morphology, contact mechanics, charge generation and external circuits. This review examines these interactions across length scales to assess how material and interface descriptions support predictive device design. Polymeric, inorganic, composite and natural materials are discussed in relation to charge generation and retention, mechanical compliance, durability and application requirements. Modelling approaches span molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations, rough-surface contact mechanics, device-scale electrostatics and equivalent circuits. Their capabilities are assessed through the inputs they require, the quantities they predict and the experimental evidence used for validation. Particular attention is given to prescribed surface charge density, idealised geometries and nominal contact-area assumptions, which constrain predictions under realistic loading conditions. Applications are organised by macroscale, milliscale and microscale device dimensions to examine requirements for materials, architecture and integration. The review identifies evolving real contact area and contact-dependent charge generation and decay as critical links between interfacial behaviour and electrical output. A staged validation strategy is proposed for contact mechanics, electrostatics and circuit response, with independent testing beyond calibration conditions. These priorities guide the development of multiscale models and reliable TENG systems.

infographic.key_insight: Predictive triboelectric nanogenerator design requires linking evolving real contact area and contact-dependent charge generation and decay to electrical output across scales.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coupling material selection, interface mechanics and circuit response can guide reliable mechanical-energy harvesting and self-powered sensing.
method: Review polymeric, inorganic, composite and natural materials against charge retention, compliance and durability requirements.
Assess modelling from molecular and first-principles calculations to contact mechanics, device electrostatics and equivalent circuits.
Organise applications by device scale and propose staged validation of contact mechanics, electrostatics and circuit response.
infographic.evidence_signal: The review assesses model inputs, predicted quantities and experimental validation evidence, and proposes independent testing beyond calibration conditions.
infographic.watch_item: Prescribed surface charge density, idealised geometries and nominal contact-area assumptions can limit predictions under realistic loading.
infographic.paper_title: Triboelectric nanogenerators across length scales: linking materials, multiscale modelling and applications

title: Agentic inverse design of spatially programmed materials
authors: Denisse Córdova Carrizales, Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk, L. Dagny Davis, Jeremy Ramsey, Ryotaro Okabe, Mouyang Cheng
abstract: Spatially programmed functional materials, from functionally graded alloys and metamaterials to quantum superlattices, use their spatial structure to tailor physical properties. However, translating a desired spatial structure into a practical fabrication recipe remains challenging due to the complex relationship between processing conditions and resulting material structures. Here we show that a large language model (LLM) agent can inverse-design such fabrication recipes by using a physics-based simulator of ion-matter interactions as a tool. Given an arbitrary depth profile of implanted ions or vacancies, the agent selects the ion species, energies, incident angles, and target material layers; writes, runs, and interprets simulations; and iteratively refines the recipe until the simulated profile matches the target, with minimal human input. Our work demonstrates physics-guided agentic inverse design as a practical approach to making the spatial structure of materials a programmable variable, opening new opportunities to explore emergent physical phenomena and functional phases of matter.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM agent uses physics-based simulations to inverse-design fabrication recipes for desired depth profiles of implanted ions or vacancies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help translate spatial material designs into ion-processing recipes for graded materials, metamaterials, and quantum superlattices.
method: Specify a target ion or vacancy depth profile.
Select ion species, energies, incident angles, and target material layers.
Write, run, and interpret ion–matter simulations, iteratively refining the recipe.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulated profile matching with minimal human input, but provides no quantitative accuracy metrics or experimental fabrication validation.
infographic.watch_item: Practical deployment requires validating that simulator-designed recipes reproduce target profiles in fabricated materials.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic inverse design of spatially programmed materials

title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys
authors: Eric A. Lass, Carla Joyce C. Nocheseda, Christopher Tandoc, Yong-Jie Hu, Peter K. Liaw
abstract: Refractory compositionally complex alloys (R-CCAs) show great promise as next generation structural materials for extreme conditions, but alloys with excellent high temperature mechanical properties most often exhibit virtually zero room temperature tensile ductility, hindering potential commercial application. Several semi-empirical metrics have been employed for predicting plasticity in R-CCAs, including valence electron concentration, Pugh ratio, Rice criteria, and the D-parameter. While many currently available ductility metrics correlate very well when compressive plasticity is considered, only the density functional theory (DFT) based D-parameter shows a strong correlation in tension. A new ductility metric is developed using CALculation of PHAse Diagrams (CALPHAD) thermodynamics, Gamma, with includes the free energy difference between the body-centered cubic (BCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phases, the interfacial free energy of a (110) BCC surface, and an electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion. The Gamma parameter exhibits better correlation with tensile ductility than D-parameter and performs equally well in compression. While this improvement is modest, a thermodynamically grounded ductility metric is clearly required to capture intrinsic ductility behavior. Extrinsic contributions to brittle behavior in R-CCAs, namely interstitial oxygen content, are also briefly discussed. Combining the Gamma ductility parameter with CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility is proposed as a first order attempt to capture both intrinsic and extrinsic contributions to ductile behavior in R-CCAs.

infographic.key_insight: The CALPHAD-based Gamma metric correlates better with tensile ductility in refractory compositionally complex alloys than the DFT-based D-parameter, while performing equally well in compression.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Gamma could help screen refractory alloys for room-temperature ductility, a key barrier to deploying these materials in extreme environments.
method: Compare existing ductility metrics against compressive and tensile plasticity.
Construct Gamma from BCC–HCP free-energy differences, BCC (110) surface interfacial free energy, and electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion.
Propose combining Gamma with CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility to capture intrinsic and extrinsic ductility effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports modestly improved correlation with tensile ductility relative to the D-parameter but provides no dataset sizes or quantitative correlation values.
infographic.watch_item: Gamma alone does not capture oxygen-related embrittlement; the proposed oxygen-solubility extension requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys

title: Data-driven candidate structure ensemble generation beyond the convex hull with crystALL approach
authors: Adam M. Krajewski, Ricardo Amaral, Jonathan W. Siegel, Luke A. Myers, Rushi Gong, Shun-Li Shang
abstract: Real materials consist of multiple stable or metastable states under real-world conditions, existing as statistical ergodic ensembles of configurations rather than ideal crystals. Yet, data-driven computational materials discovery increasingly biases itself toward finding "new stable structures" from ground-state DFT calculations alone. This limits our long-term ability to discover materials whose properties emerge from metastable phases, to explain experimental observations, or to model thermodynamic behavior comprehensively. Predicting ergodic sets of atomic configurations of known and hypothetical solids is a fundamental challenge in theoretical crystallography, approached via many complementary methods. We discuss this conceptually and introduce crystALL, a pragmatic and powerful data-driven approach to discovering ensembles beyond the convex hull, embracing structural diversity over stability alone, enabling robust experiment matching in cases evading traditional methods. crystALL leverages 5 million relaxed structures from OPTIMADE and MPDD to rapidly generate a comprehensive candidate set by: (1) species substitutions; (2) ML feature-space analysis with pySIPFENN; (3) representative structure selection via clustering and energy-minimization or property matching; and (4) construction of the final candidate ensemble for experimental or ab initio validation. We also uniquely address the common challenge of experimental composition uncertainties spanning many integer stoichiometries by new efficient searches across anonymized compositional ranges rather than fixed formulas. Overall, crystALL's ensemble-focused philosophy provides critical advantages over the prevailing convex-hull-searching paradigm, which often fails to account for key experimental observations and increases AI/ML discovery bias over time - akin to model collapse in LLMs retrained on iteratively generated content.

infographic.key_insight: crystALL prioritizes structurally diverse candidate ensembles, including metastable configurations beyond the convex hull, rather than searching only for stable ground-state structures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Broader candidate ensembles can support experimental structure identification and investigation of materials whose properties depend on metastable phases.
method: Generate candidates through species substitutions and searches across anonymized composition ranges.
Analyze candidates in ML feature space with pySIPFENN and cluster to select representatives.
Use energy minimization or property matching to assemble ensembles for experimental or ab initio validation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach draws on 5 million relaxed structures from OPTIMADE and MPDD, but the abstract reports no quantitative accuracy or speed benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Candidate diversity does not establish thermodynamic populations or kinetic accessibility; generated ensembles require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Data-driven candidate structure ensemble generation beyond the convex hull with crystALL approach

title: Statistically Robust Characterization of Polaron and Bipolaron Intrinsic Traps in Amorphous Silica Reveals the Role of Network Flexibility in Electron Localisation
authors: Robin Delhomme, Jonathon Cottom, Emilia Olsson
abstract: Intrinsic electron localization in amorphous silica (a-SiO2) contributes to charge trapping and defect generation in silica-based electronic materials - a phenomenon that degrades logic-device performance but can be exploited for memory applications. However, the structural distribution of one- and two-electron traps remains incompletely characterized, largely because the disordered covalent network of a-SiO2 spans a vast configurational space. To address this, we perform statistical sampling to select a representative 200-model subset of defect-free bulk a-SiO2 structures from a structurally converged parent set of 2512 models, generated via classical melt-quench molecular dynamics simulations. We then characterize the intrinsic one- and two-electron traps in this subset using HSE06 density functional theory calculations. Analysis of neutral precursor sites shows that trapping propensity is not determined by a universal O-Si-O angle or Si-O bond length; it is controlled by the accessibility of the relaxed trap geometry, requiring both local strain and medium-range network flexibility. Single electrons predominantly form edge-centred polarons on distorted SiO4 tetrahedra, with occupied states 3.1-4.3 eV below the conduction band minimum. Injection of a second electron drives stronger lattice relaxation, most commonly Si-O bond elongation leading to rupture, thereby forming threefold-coordinated-Si (Si3) bipolarons and, in some cases, Si-Si-bonded bipolaron configurations. The calculated bipolaron energy ranges are consistent with optical absorption features at 3.7, 4.7, and 6.4 eV associated with intrinsic electron localization.

infographic.key_insight: Intrinsic electron trapping in amorphous silica depends on local strain and medium-range network flexibility, not a universal bond-length or bond-angle threshold.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding these traps can inform efforts to mitigate charge-trapping degradation in silica-based logic devices or exploit it in memory applications.
method: Generate 2,512 defect-free amorphous silica models using classical melt-quench molecular dynamics.
Statistically select a representative 200-model subset.
Use HSE06 density functional theory to characterize one- and two-electron trapping.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the sampled structures, single-electron polaron states lie 3.1–4.3 eV below the conduction band minimum, while calculated bipolaron energy ranges are consistent with optical absorption features at 3.7, 4.7, and 6.4 eV.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern defect-free bulk models; transferability to device interfaces, pre-existing defects, and operating conditions requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Statistically Robust Characterization of Polaron and Bipolaron Intrinsic Traps in Amorphous Silica Reveals the Role of Network Flexibility in Electron Localisation

title: Nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulation with external field
authors: Chengji Li, Fan Zheng
abstract: Nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations with classical path approximation (CPA-NAMD) cannot simulate the carrier dynamics under an external field. We develop CPA-NAMD-extF, a first-principles density-matrix framework for calculating field-driven electronic responses along precomputed finite-temperature ionic trajectories. The method combines explicit external-field coupling with self-consistent updates of electronic density while retaining the computational efficiency of the classical-path approximation. Benchmarks against regular TDDFT methods show close agreement for time-dependent dipoles, finite-field currents, and linear optical responses. Applications to the linear absorption spectrum of crystalline and amorphous SiO$_2$ demonstrate its capability to large and structurally complex systems. This method is also applied to the 2D hybrid perovskite $(\mathrm{BA})_2\mathrm{CsPb}_2\mathrm{Br}_7$. Finite-temperature calculations show that the second-order opto-current response is strongly affected by structural fluctuations. Real-space DC current density further reveals pronounced Br-centered vortex currents, and its microscopic origin is investigated.

infographic.key_insight: CPA-NAMD-extF extends classical-path nonadiabatic molecular dynamics to simulate field-driven electronic responses while retaining computational efficiency.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables finite-temperature optical and current-response calculations for large, structurally complex materials.
method: Evolve a first-principles electronic density matrix along precomputed finite-temperature ionic trajectories.
Include explicit external-field coupling and self-consistent electronic-density updates.
Apply the framework to crystalline and amorphous SiO₂ and a 2D hybrid perovskite.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks show close agreement with regular TDDFT for time-dependent dipoles, finite-field currents, and linear optical responses; perovskite calculations reveal fluctuation-sensitive second-order opto-currents and Br-centered vortex currents.
infographic.watch_item: Precomputed ionic trajectories retain the classical-path approximation, so field-induced feedback on ionic motion may require separate validation.
infographic.paper_title: Nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulation with external field

title: TT-SCHA for Thermodynamics of Binary Alloys
authors: Boian S. Alexandrov, Dimiter Petsev
abstract: The free energy of a crystal is an integral over the positions of all its atoms, in 3N dimensions. We evaluate it without random sampling for the ordered alloys B2 NiAl and gamma-TiAl with embedded-atom potentials, using a self-consistent harmonic approximation (SCHA) corrected to third order in temperature, calculated via thermal averages of tensor-train (TT) integrals built from one atom and its neighbors, which we call TT-SCHA. The result is for an infinite crystal without sampling error; its numerical error is set by the starting pivots of the interpolation (up to 9 MPa in the pressure, reduced by averaging three runs; SM Table S26). Against the molecular dynamics of 65,536 atoms (Frenkel-Ladd free energy at 600 K, integrated energy above), TT-SCHA free energy agrees to 0.13 meV per atom at 600-1000 K, using 420-500 times fewer core-seconds for one run. At zero pressure, results agree with published calculations that use the same embedded-atom potential: the published elastic constants of gamma-TiAl (to 1 GPa, by a static lattice calculation) and its thermal expansion from Monte Carlo sampling (to 0.012 percentage points).

infographic.key_insight: TT-SCHA computes binary-alloy crystal free energies without random sampling, matching molecular dynamics within 0.13 meV per atom at 600–1000 K.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers efficient thermodynamic evaluation of ordered alloys, using 420–500 times fewer core-seconds per run than the molecular-dynamics benchmark.
method: Model B2 NiAl and gamma-TiAl with embedded-atom potentials.
Apply a self-consistent harmonic approximation corrected to third order in temperature.
Evaluate thermal averages using tensor-train integrals over one atom and its neighbors.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation used 65,536-atom molecular dynamics and same-potential published results, with gamma-TiAl elastic constants agreeing within 1 GPa and thermal expansion within 0.012 percentage points.
infographic.watch_item: Sampling error is absent, but interpolation starting pivots introduce numerical variability of up to 9 MPa in pressure, reduced by averaging three runs.
infographic.paper_title: TT-SCHA for Thermodynamics of Binary Alloys

title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
authors: Suhas Suresh Bharadwaj
abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed neural network with exact boundary and initial constraints recovers the shear piezoelectric coefficient e15 accurately from sparse, noisy simulated wavefields.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could enable non-destructive characterization of shear-mode coupling for PMUT and surface acoustic wave devices without dedicated resonance-test specimens.
method: Embed spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers in network outputs to enforce boundary and initial conditions exactly.
Train on coupled electro-elastodynamic equations and sparse observations, without boundary or initial-condition penalty weights.
Non-dimensionalize the governing equations to improve coefficient scaling.
infographic.evidence_signal: On finite-element data sampled along one subsurface line, the full formulation achieved 1.19% mean e15 error at 30 dB noise and 0.65–2.71% across a 40–0 dB noise sweep.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is simulation-only; robustness to experimental measurements, uncertain boundary conditions, and material-model mismatch remains untested.
infographic.paper_title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints

title: Machine Learning Aided Computational Discovery of Boride Substrates for Borophene Synthesis
authors: Luqing Wang, Qunfei Zhou, Qiucheng Li, Venkata Surya Chaitanya Kolluru, Hui Li, Albert Tsui
abstract: Borophene, a monolayer of boron, is distinctive among two-dimensional materials owing to its unique properties, including polymorphism and potential applications in quantum technologies and energy conversion and storage. Nevertheless, its applications are hindered by the strong binding of borophene to metal substrates, which impedes the realization of freestanding borophene. Alternative substrates with tunable binding to borophene are therefore highly desirable. Since boride layers arise during borophene synthesis on metals, borides provide potential alternative substrates for borophene synthesis. In this work, we investigate the binding energies and interactions between borophene and 1356 boride surfaces for two borophene phases (v1/6 and v1/9), using density functional theory (DFT) calculations and machine learning (ML). Importantly, incorporating ML-predicted charge transfer as an input feature to a subsequent ML model enables physics-informed predictions of binding energies. Additional DFT calculations on four representative cases were performed to validate the ML predictions. SHAP analysis reveals that the majority of key descriptors are associated with delocalized electrons, highlighting the role of electronic properties in governing binding strength. Combined DFT and ML screening identifies 65 and 73 promising boride surfaces for the v1/6 and v1/9 phases, respectively. Al- and Ag-based borides, including AlB2 and AgB2, emerge as predominant candidates for both phases. The computationally predicted candidate substrates and the deduced design guidelines provide a charge-transfer-informed ML strategy for substrate selection and represent promising steps toward the experimental realization of freestanding borophene.

infographic.key_insight: Charge-transfer-informed machine learning identifies boride substrates with promising borophene binding, with Al- and Ag-based borides emerging as leading candidates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tuning substrate binding could support borophene synthesis and eventual release for quantum and energy applications.
method: Combine DFT and ML to screen 1,356 boride surfaces for two borophene phases, ν1/6 and ν1/9.
Use ML-predicted charge transfer as an input to a subsequent binding-energy model.
Apply SHAP analysis to identify influential descriptors, highlighting delocalized-electron properties.
infographic.evidence_signal: Screening identified 65 promising surfaces for ν1/6 and 73 for ν1/9, with additional DFT calculations on four representative cases used to validate ML predictions.
infographic.watch_item: The candidates remain computational predictions; experimental synthesis and borophene release require validation.
infographic.paper_title: Machine Learning Aided Computational Discovery of Boride Substrates for Borophene Synthesis

title: Surrogate Models for Stochastic Al-Cu Phase-Field Solidification
authors: Simon Savukoski, Tatu Pinomaa
abstract: Phase-field models resolve microstructural evolution during rapid alloy solidification, but their computational cost limits long trajectories, stochastic ensembles, and studies across process conditions. We present a variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge model (VP-DDBM) for state-conditioned prediction of two-dimensional Al-Cu solidification. Given the current phase, concentration, and prescribed temperature fields, the model predicts the subsequent state and is applied autoregressively. Across two held-out thermal gradients, VP-DDBM produces lower long-horizon errors than deterministic U-Net and SI-ConvNeXt baselines in domain-mean phase, domain-mean Cu concentration, and leading-tip position. It also retains fine dendritic structure over long rollouts, whereas the deterministic U-Net progressively smooths the morphology. VP-DDBM predicts the phase and concentration evolution approximately $73\times$ faster than the phase-field solver, showing potential for faster process-condition screening and ensemble-based microstructure studies.

infographic.key_insight: A variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge model predicts stochastic Al–Cu solidification while retaining fine dendritic structure and running approximately 73× faster than the phase-field solver.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster microstructure prediction could enable broader process-condition screening and ensemble studies of rapid alloy solidification.
method: Condition VP-DDBM on current phase, Cu concentration, and prescribed temperature fields.
Predict the next two-dimensional phase and concentration state.
Apply predictions autoregressively to generate long rollouts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two held-out thermal gradients, VP-DDBM achieved lower long-horizon errors than deterministic U-Net and SI-ConvNeXt baselines in mean phase, mean Cu concentration, and leading-tip position.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to two-dimensional simulations and two held-out thermal gradients; broader process and three-dimensional generalization remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Surrogate Models for Stochastic Al-Cu Phase-Field Solidification

title: Learning from high-resolution 2D images to reconstruct 3D microstructures
authors: Wenbo Sui, Lars P. Mikkelsen, Jens W. Andreasen, Daniel Lichau, Harold Phelippeau, Philip J. Withers
abstract: High-resolution three-dimensional (3D) microstructure characterization remains difficult to undertake at scale because volumetric imaging at the required spatial resolution is expensive, time-consuming or destructive. In many settings, however, fine-resolution two-dimensional (2D) imaging and lower-resolution volumetric measurements are both readily available. We introduce a Privileged Cross-modal Relational Distillation (PCRD) framework that leverages fine-resolution 2D observations during training to improve specimen-specific 3D reconstruction from lower-resolution volumetric imaging alone. We demonstrate PCRD on pultruded carbon fiber-reinforced polymer composites, using scanning electron microscopy as the privileged modality and micro-CT as the inference input. The framework transfers spatial organization by matching similarity distributions defined around corresponding spatial anchors in the teacher and student representations, avoiding direct alignment of heterogeneous feature vectors. In 2D cross-sectional reconstruction, PCRD improves mAP by 1.66 percentage points over direct micro-CT training. Independent 3D validation against high-resolution synchrotron X-ray CT data shows close agreement in fiber volume fraction, diameter and local spacing. The PCRD reconstruction matches 89.97% of the reference fiber centerline length, compared with 75.08% for the interpolated low-resolution volume.

infographic.key_insight: Privileged Cross-modal Relational Distillation (PCRD) uses high-resolution 2D images during training to improve specimen-specific 3D microstructure reconstruction from lower-resolution volumetric imaging alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce reliance on expensive high-resolution 3D imaging when characterizing fiber architecture in carbon fiber-reinforced polymer composites.
method: Use scanning electron microscopy as the privileged training modality and micro-CT as the inference input.
Transfer spatial organization by matching teacher–student similarity distributions around corresponding spatial anchors.
Avoid direct alignment of heterogeneous feature vectors.
infographic.evidence_signal: In pultruded carbon fiber composites, PCRD improved 2D mAP by 1.66 percentage points over direct micro-CT training and matched 89.97% of reference fiber centerline length in independent synchrotron CT validation, versus 75.08% for the interpolated low-resolution volume.
infographic.watch_item: Training requires corresponding spatial anchors across modalities, and generalization beyond the demonstrated composite system remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Learning from high-resolution 2D images to reconstruct 3D microstructures

title: High-Entropy A-Site Disorder Enhances Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity and Stability in Nickelate Thin Films
authors: Min-Ju Choi, Le Wang, Krishna Prasad Koirala, Hyoju Park, Mark E. Bowden, Elizabeth Helen Krenkel
abstract: Rare-earth nickelates are among the most active oxide electrocatalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), owing to their tunable Ni-O covalency, near-unity eg occupancy, and sensitivity to A-site chemistry, oxygen stoichiometry, and epitaxial strain. Here, we use epitaxial A-site high-entropy (La0.2Pr0.2Nd0.2Sm0.2Eu0.2)NiO3 thin films to reveal how epitaxial strain influences defect formation, Ni valence, electronic structure, and OER activity in a chemically disordered rare-earth (RE) sublattice. Tensile strain promotes Ruddlesden-Popper fault formation, interrupts the corner-sharing NiO6 network, and lowers the average Ni oxidation state. Although the occupied density of states near the Fermi level remains largely unchanged, O K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy reveals increased low-energy unoccupied states under tensile strain. First-principles calculations suggest that tensile strain shifts RE 4f-derived states toward the Fermi level, enhancing RE 4f-O 2p-Ni 3d hybridization. These coupled structural and electronic changes lead to earlier OER onset, stronger pre-catalytic Ni redox features, and higher activity than compressively strained films and representative single-A-site nickelates. The high-entropy nickelate also shows enhanced resistance to OER-induced structural degradation compared with LaNiO3. These results suggest that A-site configurational disorder and epitaxial strain can jointly tune defect formation and rare-earth-derived electronic states, providing a route for improving perovskite oxide electrocatalysts.

infographic.key_insight: A-site high-entropy disorder and tensile strain jointly tune nickelate defects and electronic states, improving oxygen evolution activity while enhancing structural durability relative to LaNiO3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining compositional disorder with epitaxial strain offers a route to engineer more active, degradation-resistant perovskite oxide electrocatalysts.
method: Study epitaxial (La0.2Pr0.2Nd0.2Sm0.2Eu0.2)NiO3 films under different strain conditions.
Characterize structural faults, Ni valence, electronic states, and electrochemical OER response.
Use first-principles calculations to interpret strain-dependent rare-earth orbital hybridization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tensile-strained films show earlier OER onset, stronger pre-catalytic Ni redox features, and higher activity than compressively strained films and representative single-A-site nickelates; the high-entropy material better resists structural degradation than LaNiO3.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative activity or durability metrics, and transferability from epitaxial films to practical catalyst architectures remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: High-Entropy A-Site Disorder Enhances Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity and Stability in Nickelate Thin Films

title: Methodological Assessment of Instrumented Indentation for Spatially Resolved Mesoscale Stiffness and Creep in Short Fiber-Reinforced Injection-Molded PBT Components
authors: Eduard Klatt, Natalie Rauter
abstract: Instrumented indentation enables assessment of local mechanical properties in heterogeneous polymer systems, but specimen preparation and the selected indentation protocol significantly influence the quantitative interpretation of the measured response. This study develops and evaluates an experimental methodology for spatially resolved mesoscale characterization of both unreinforced and short fiber-reinforced composites. An unreinforced material system is used as a reference material to systematically examine the effects of indentation spacing, surface preparation, maximum indentation load, temporal loading parameters, and unloading evaluation. Indentation loads of 500, 1000, and 1750 mN are investigated in complementary experimental campaigns. The apparent indentation modulus exhibits moderate sensitivity to indentation load and loading time within the studied ranges. In contrast, indentation depth and the creep-related depth increment display greater sensitivity to the applied load history. Surface polishing minimizes topographical disturbances and enables reliable identification of residual indentation profiles and pile-up. Based on these methodological findings, a final load-hold-unload protocol with an indentation load of 1750 mN, a loading time of 6 s, a holding period of 300 s, and an unloading time of 4 s is applied to both unreinforced material and short fiber-reinforced composites. The mean apparent indentation modulus increases from 2.91 GPa for unreinforced material to 6.65 GPa for short fiber-reinforced composites, while the mean depth of indentation creep decreases from 2.36 to 1.91 microns. The coefficient of variation also increases for both quantities, indicating that short-fiber reinforcement enhances mean local stiffness and introduces pronounced spatial heterogeneity in both stiffness-related and time-dependent mesoscale indentation responses.

infographic.key_insight: Short-fiber reinforcement increases mean local apparent indentation modulus in PBT while reducing mean indentation creep depth and increasing spatial heterogeneity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A controlled indentation protocol enables spatially resolved stiffness and creep assessment in heterogeneous injection-molded PBT components.
method: Use unreinforced PBT to assess indentation spacing, surface preparation, load, timing, and unloading evaluation.
Compare indentation loads of 500, 1000, and 1750 mN; polish surfaces to reduce topographical disturbances.
Apply a final 1750 mN protocol with 6 s loading, 300 s holding, and 4 s unloading to unreinforced and short-fiber-reinforced PBT.
infographic.evidence_signal: Mean apparent indentation modulus increases from 2.91 to 6.65 GPa, mean creep depth decreases from 2.36 to 1.91 µm, and coefficients of variation increase for both quantities with reinforcement.
infographic.watch_item: Quantitative results depend on surface preparation and load history; apparent indentation modulus should not be treated as protocol-independent bulk stiffness.
infographic.paper_title: Methodological Assessment of Instrumented Indentation for Spatially Resolved Mesoscale Stiffness and Creep in Short Fiber-Reinforced Injection-Molded PBT Components

title: Quantum 3xplorer: AI-Native Engine for Next-Generation Quantum Materials Modeling
authors: Vsevolod Biryukov, Sergey V. Barabash, Pranab Kumar Das, Jack Deslippe, Mauro Del Ben, Felipe H. da Jornada
abstract: Quantum-mechanical approaches, such as density functional theory (DFT), underpin much of modern computational materials science and are the primary source of data for AI-driven discovery. Yet the established electronic-structure codes today represent decades-old software architectures, making new physical models slow and costly to implement, validate, and deploy on emerging hardware. We present Quantum 3xplorer (Q3, pronounced "Quantum Explorer"), an AI-native quantum simulation engine written from scratch by AI coding agents under the direction and supervision of domain scientists. As a first and demanding validation case, we implement plane-wave pseudopotential DFT end to end: norm-conserving, ultrasoft, and projector-augmented-wave formalisms, spin polarization, DFT+U, and dispersion corrections, together with forces, stresses, structural relaxation, and electronic-structure analysis. Q3 reproduces established reference implementations, runs faster on a single core in representative benchmarks, and scales across GPU-accelerated supercomputers. It was developed in weeks rather than years. Its layered, physics-first architecture separates abstract quantum-mechanical concepts from their numerical representations, making its framework extendable beyond plane waves to other basis sets and levels of theory. Its inputs and outputs follow structured, schema-validated data standards, making every result AI-ready. Q3 is open source under Apache 2.0 and built to be reused, extended, and improved by the research community. Q3 points to a paradigm shift in how computational quantum science is done. Scientists define the physics, formulate the models, and set the criteria for validation; AI agents write, test, and optimize the code. The decades-long path from a new theory to a trusted, high-performance implementation can thus collapse to days, significantly accelerating scientific discovery.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum 3xplorer (Q3) demonstrates scientist-supervised, AI-agent development of a quantum simulation engine, implementing a broad plane-wave DFT feature set in weeks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its layered architecture, schema-validated inputs and outputs, and GPU scaling support extensible, AI-ready materials simulation workflows.
method: Scientists define physics and validation criteria; AI agents write, test, and optimize code.
Implement plane-wave pseudopotential DFT with spin polarization, DFT+U, dispersion corrections, forces, and stresses.
Separate quantum-mechanical abstractions from numerical representations to support future extensions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports agreement with established reference implementations, faster single-core execution in representative benchmarks, and scaling across GPU-accelerated supercomputers.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical accuracy tolerances, benchmark details, or scaling efficiencies, limiting assessment of performance generality.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum 3xplorer: AI-Native Engine for Next-Generation Quantum Materials Modeling

title: Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data
authors: Arda Uzunoglu, Mahler Revsine, Michael Schatz, Benjamin Van Durme, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Daniel Khashabi
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise for scientific discovery, yet basic questions remain about what enables reliable discovery. How can we trace the scientific discovery capacity of LLMs to their training data? We study this question as one of missing probability mass and develop a theoretical account in which monofacts-the facts observed once during training-set the discovery capacity. In materials science and regulatory genomics, we directly manipulate monofact rates in training sets and find that more monofacts consistently yield more discoveries across two open-weight model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets. Further experiments show the relationship cannot be explained by training-set diversity alone and can transfer across scientific domains when paired with in-domain data. Together, our results identify monofact rate in training data as a key factor governing discoveries in language models.

infographic.key_insight: Facts seen only once during training—called monofacts—help govern an LLM’s capacity for scientific discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Training-data design that accounts for monofact rates could improve LLM-assisted materials discovery.
method: Model discovery capacity through missing probability mass.
Directly manipulate monofact rates in training data.
Test discovery across model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: In materials science and regulatory genomics, higher monofact rates consistently yielded more discoveries across two open-weight model families, with effects not explained by training-set diversity alone.
infographic.watch_item: Cross-domain transfer was demonstrated when paired with in-domain data, so monofact enrichment should not be assumed to replace domain-specific training.
infographic.paper_title: Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data
